transcript:
"This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour."
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Herbst.
Recently, reinstalled Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is set to appear before a congressional panel
in a closed-door meeting next week.
He resigned after reports of affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy.
But this week, the chipmaker reinstalled him after President Trump intervened.
Many questions and concerns from both sides of the aisle remain about the national security
scandal that led to his ouster.
Republican Congressman Brian Fitzpatrick, who sits on the House Intelligence Committee,
has more on what the panel wants to know.
"This is a typical FBI protocol for anybody in the private sector that is in what we call
critical infrastructure or critical industry, whether it be artificial intelligence, quantum
computing, machine learning, semiconductors, to be briefed by the FBI of the threats that
may be headed their way in terms of intelligence and counterintelligence.
So the question is, did Jensen and people at Nvidia get this defensive briefing in advance?"
Speaking there on NPR's Morning Edition, shares of Nvidia are down 5 percent in pre-market
trading.
Kilmar Abrego-Garcia has self-deported and is now in Spain.
The Salvadoran immigrant became a symbol of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown
after he was wrongly deported and then brought back to the U.S.
And here's Juliana Kim has more.
Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen wrote on X that "Kilmar is traveling to a country of
his choice, a free man, unharmed and with dignity."
The Democrat has played a leading role in championing Abrego-Garcia's case since last
year, when the man who had been living in Maryland was deported to El Salvador by mistake.
The details of Abrego-Garcia's voluntary departure are unclear, but it comes after
months of sparring with the Trump administration.
Abrego-Garcia said he was willing to move to Costa Rica, but the federal government
did not support those plans and instead sought to deport him to a country in Africa.
Juliana Kim, NPR News.
All six people on board a small plane have been killed after the Cessna went down yesterday
in the Gulf of Mexico off the coast of Mississippi.
Here's Matt Bloom reports the U.S. Coast Guard says those killed include two children.
The Cessna was en route from New Orleans to Fort Myers, Florida, when it suddenly lost
contact with a regional air traffic control tower.
The Coast Guard says crews searched for the missing plane for four hours.
The search concluded when divers located the aircraft's fuselage between Pascagoula and
Horn Island.
The area is part of the Gulf Islands national seashore.
The Coast Guard said all six victims were accounted for.
The Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transportation Safety Board are expected
to investigate what caused the crash.
Matt Bloom, NPR News.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
In Saudi Arabia, 11 people were injured yesterday in an attack on a high-rise tower in the capital's
financial district.
It's the second Houthi attack on the public investment fund tower in less than a week.
The kingdom is blaming the attack on the Iran-backed Houthis who are targeting Saudi oil sites,
airports, and Riyadh's financial district with missiles and drones.
The Houthis say they also struck Saudi Arabia's largest oil refinery in the east, sparking
fires there.
Saudi air strikes, meanwhile, are targeting the Houthis across Yemen daily.
For decades, the vitamin K injection has been a standard part of hospital care for newborns.
It prevents rare hemorrhages that can be fatal.
But as more patients are declining the vitamin K for their babies, doctors are trying to
change their minds.
Kate Wells from KFF Health News has more.
The rate of newborns not getting the vitamin K injection in the U.S. has more than doubled
in recent years.
And at Helen DeVos Children's Hospital in Grand Rapids, Michigan, Dr. Tori LeBlanc saw
more babies develop life-threatening bleeds as a result.
"But you can't let your anger or your feelings impact your conversation with the family because
they can feel that, then they're not as willing to listen to what you have to say."
Over the last two years, LeBlanc says about 50% of the parents that she's talked to have
changed their minds after initially declining vitamin K.
Kate Wells with our partner KFF Health News.
U.S. futures contracts are trading lower at this hour.
NASDAQ futures are down nearly 3%.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
This message comes from Rosetta Stone, offering an alternative approach to language learning.
The app guides users to intuitively think in a second language using images and contextual
audio, mimicking how people acquire speech as children.
The platform also includes advanced speech recognition technology that compares a learner's
pronunciation directly with native speakers to refine accent precision.
Learn more about their immersion method and the new Rosetta Stone Sapphire app at RosettaStone.com.

topics.text: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to appear before congressional panel in closed-door meeting next week
Kilmar Abrego-Garcia self-deports to Spain after months of dispute with Trump administration
Six killed when Cessna plane crashes in Gulf of Mexico off Mississippi coast, including two children
Eleven injured in Houthi attack on high-rise tower in Saudi Arabia's Riyadh financial district
Rate of newborns skipping vitamin K injection rises; doctors work to change parents' minds
U.S. stock futures fall sharply in early trading, with NASDAQ futures down nearly 3%
